title: Workshop Maintenance Planning
body: At ADW the daily availability report can read 90%-plus and still hide a rotting backlog — because a unit that's been down 60, 100, or 216 days simply drops out of the active count. If you're only watching the A&U number, you're blind to exactly the machines costing the most.
keyPoints: The Workshop Daily Task sheet has four blocks — daily maintenance/greasing, scheduled services, the breakdown register, and welding — and the breakdown register is where the real backlog lives, not the availability report.
Anything tagged "waiting decision" is not a parts or labor problem — it's a repair-or-replace call nobody has made. Chase the decision-maker, not the workshop.

External-supplier dependency is the long pole every time. A part sitting at Zahid or another outside shop for weeks or months needs its own escalation path — it isn't a workshop-capacity issue, so leaning on the workshop won't move it.

Generators and site infrastructure carry standing faults too, and because they're not production fleet, they never show up in the A&U view. No one is tracking spare power margin until a second unit fails.

The forward weekly schedule and the daily task sheet can legitimately disagree with what the availability report shows as completed — read the plan and the actual together, never one instead of the other.
apply: Before you sign off on any long-down unit, ask what stage it's actually stuck at — parts, labor, or an undecided repair-or-replace call — because each one needs a different push, and the wrong push wastes another day.
